summary.text: The received pictographic account relates 了 to 子 without arms, though this reading is disputed. The graph is also used for “finish”; whether it was reused because the depicted form’s old name sounded similar, or whether the meanings developed through entanglement and tying, remains unresolved.

formation.text: The received account treats 了 as a whole pictograph related to 子 with its arms omitted. A separate commentary interprets the graph as crossed or entangled legs. These are competing readings of the graph, not confirmed depictions of an early inscription.

components.text: The graph as a whole is interpreted in the received account as 子 without arms. This is a disputed pictorial reading; the evidence does not confirm the referent of an early inscription.

history.text: The received account relates the graph to 子; later commentary reads it as crossed or entangled legs. The cited evidence establishes no securely dated earliest form or sequence of graphic changes. The selected seal-style image is a modern redraw of the received dictionary form, not an ancient artifact or evidence that resolves these interpretations.

uncertainties.text: The use of 了 for “finish” has been explained either as sound-based reuse of a sign for a word that sounded alike or similar, or through a proposed path from entanglement to tying and completion. The old name and any sound match are unverified, and no dated examples establish the proposed semantic steps.

Accounts trace the completed-action particle to Tang–Song usage, but the cited summaries provide no dated primary examples. A possible interaction between sentence-final 了 and 也 in some dialects remains tentative.

senses.text: The received entry glosses 了 with 尦; later commentary interprets this as legs crossing or becoming entangled. This is a historical interpretation, not direct confirmation of what an early inscription depicted.

Historical dictionary citations include “finish; be completed”; a Tang poem uses 未了 for “not ended” or “not finished.” The earliest attestation and the connection between this meaning and the graphic interpretations remain unresolved.
